transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for having me. Um, honestly, what made me finally come in is that I just keep getting up during our long sales strategy meetings. Like, I know I’m supposed to just stay seated and listen, but I always end up getting up to refill my water or just... pace by the printer. 

Which, actually, the printer on our floor has been an absolute nightmare lately. It jams almost every single time we try to print the glossy mockups for our ad pitches. My clients—I handle a lot of mid-size tech startups right now—they really expect these physical pitch decks to look absolutely perfect, so it's incredibly stressful when the toner smears. I spent like twenty minutes on the phone with IT on Tuesday just trying to get them to send a tech out. But anyway, yeah, even when the printer is fine, I just can't seem to stay in my chair when we have those long meetings.
Do you remember having this same kind of restlessness or trouble sitting still back when you were a kid in school, or is this something that's really only started more recently as an adult?

Oh, no, it definitely isn't a new thing. It started way before high school. I actually know this for a fact because I just found some of my old report cards when I was helping my mom clean out her attic last weekend. She lives in this gorgeous old Victorian house, but the dust up there is just unbelievable. I was sneezing for two days straight. We were actually up there trying to find my grandmother's vintage sewing machine—my sister is super into making her own clothes right now, which is cool, but she buys the most expensive fabrics. 

But anyway, the report cards! Yeah, my elementary school teachers always wrote the exact same thing. They’d say I was bright, but that I always rushed through my work and talked out of turn. And I was constantly forgetting my homework. My desk was just a total disaster zone, stuffed with all these half-finished papers. 

Which is kind of funny because my desk at work right now is actually pretty organized... well, mostly because everything is digital. If I had to deal with actual paper files for my clients, I don't even know what I'd do. We switched to this new CRM software last month that's supposed to keep everything paperless, but honestly the interface is so clunky, it takes me twice as long to log my calls. Half the sales team is threatening to just go back to using Excel spreadsheets. But, um... yeah, so it's definitely been happening since I was little.
Aside from the restlessness, do you currently have trouble staying focused on tasks—like losing track of what someone's saying in a meeting, or frequently forgetting details or deadlines at work?

Yeah, um, definitely. Especially with the long strategy meetings. I'll sit down and be totally locked in at first, like, okay, ready to go. But then, I don't know, a few minutes go by and I'll realize I've just been staring at the exact same slide or reading the same paragraph of a client brief over and over, and I have literally zero idea what the last point even was. 

Which is so frustrating because the briefs we've been getting lately from this one new client—this organic pet food startup—are just ridiculously long. Like, who needs a forty-page deck about grain-free kibble? I mean, I love dogs, I have a golden retriever mix named Buster who is just the absolute best, but he will eat literal garbage if I let him. He got into the trash last week and ate half a plastic container of hummus. The vet bill was insane. My husband was so mad, mostly because it was his favorite garlic hummus from that little deli down the street. They make the best sandwiches there, too. 

But, wait, what was I... right, losing track. Yeah, so I'll be looking at the pet food brief and suddenly realize I haven't absorbed a single word for the last ten minutes.

Would you say these attention and restlessness issues have actually caused real problems for you—like at work with deadlines or performance reviews, or in your relationship at home—not just been a minor annoyance?

Yeah, it... it really has. I mean, it's not just a minor thing anymore. At work, it’s actually started showing up in my performance reviews, which really sucks because I do care a lot about my job. But there was this one client complaint recently that honestly terrified me. I realized I could actually damage these accounts, even though I’m trying so hard to do good work. 

And, you know, the client who complained was actually from that same pet food startup I was just talking about. They were so mad because I missed a deadline on their Q3 projection report. Which, to be fair, their Q3 projections were completely unrealistic anyway. They wanted to expand into like fifty new boutique pet stores by November, and I kept trying to tell them that boutique store owners are incredibly picky about shelf space. My friend Sarah actually opened a little boutique pet shop downtown—well, it was downtown, but then the rent got hiked up so she had to move it to the east side. The new location is actually really cute, it has this exposed brick wall that she painted teal. She sells these hand-knitted dog sweaters that are just adorable. I bought one for Buster, but he hates wearing clothes, he just freezes and refuses to walk. 

But anyway... yeah, the client was really upset, and it made me realize that this is actually affecting my work and client trust, not just annoying me.
